title: The comparison: the two main estimates

headline.label: BSZ main estimate and JR main estimate, on the common output (b)
headline.definition: the two analyses' own main estimates, next to each other: BSZ's net total (wealth tax + extra income tax from selling assets - income tax lost to leavers, present value of 5 years) and JR's NBER September 2026 mean NPV (perpetuity). Under the common output (b), the net fiscal effect, they are the bridge's two ends, $106.8B and −$39.0B (the exact expectation of the Monte Carlo whose seeded run is −$38.886B). The gap between the ends, $145.8B, is the sum of the bridge's 10 steps

verified_by: Rscript, layer 6 at b794a9f: score_common(bridge_inputs(read_contracts())$sup)[['b']] = 106.796, the same at $rauh = -38.980, and rauh_nber_expectation(0, 72, 0.3, 0.6, 3.3, 5.8, 0.015, 0.045)[['b']] = -38.980; the same from export/r/ends.csv (bsz_model, rauh_own on (b)), from export/py/ends.csv, and from the headline and the end bars in assets/comparison-data.js. The JR main estimate as shown, −$38.886B, is the JR contract row npv_mc_nber_mean (the authors' seeded run), traced by the JR chain
runs_for_a_stranger: AUDIT.md step 8, level 2: .github/workflows/comparison-ci.yml rebuilds the comparison in R and Python on a clean runner; no one-click (Binder) yet.

# Environment for the comparison chain, R. In Positron open the opa-prop40 folder, then run this once.
# Needs nothing downloaded: the two analyses' export contracts are committed.

invisible(lapply(list.files("comparison/R", pattern = "\\.R$", full.names = TRUE), source))   # every function on the chain

layers.name: The numbers on the explorer
layers.what: This layer is the explorer's own JavaScript, not R or Python. The R and Python code starts at layer 3. The page loads the bridge's data file and prints the two main estimates from its headline object. headline.bsz is the BSZ net total. headline.rjkdc is the JR NBER mean NPV as the JR pipeline reproduces the authors' seeded run. Below them sit two panels of dials, one per analysis, in two boxes: the wealth tax collected and the income tax lost. Each dial has 5 positions. Position 0 is the panel's own analysis's value and position 4 the other analysis's. 7 inputs have a dial each. The other 3 (noncitizens, real_estate, asset_sales) share one on/off switch, which expand() turns into positions. positions() reads a panel's dials. updatePanel() calls model.js (window.ComparisonModel, a JavaScript copy of score_common() and slider_inputs(), layer 6, checked against R by test-site.R) and prints the panel's estimate and each dial's value. drawBars() draws the two panels' estimates as two bars on a fixed scale. With every dial at position 0 the two bars are the bridge's two ends. The BSZ end is the same number as the BSZ main estimate. The JR end is the exact expectation of the same Monte Carlo, a little below the seeded run. The static header carries the two main estimates too, written by site.R (layer 3), so it reads the same with JavaScript off.
layers.inputs: D = window.__BRIDGE__ from assets/comparison-data.js (D.headline; D.sliders: the two input vectors, the number of steps, the horizon settings, one entry per input and the minor inputs); M = model.js

inputs_from.what: window.__BRIDGE__: the headline object and the sliders object

layers.other_inputs: the dials' positions, set by the reader
layers.outputs: headline: '$106.8B' (BSZ main estimate) and '−$38.9B' (JR main estimate); bars with every dial at 0: '$106.8B' (BSZ panel) and '−$39.0B' (JR panel)
layers.method_ref: Display only. The definitions are the method: BSZ's net total is the wealth tax plus extra income tax from asset sales minus 5 years of lost income tax. JR's is the mean NPV in perpetuity. The footnote on the explorer says the common output (b) puts both on one definition, of which the two bars at position 0 are the ends.

r.symbol: positions(), expand(), updatePanel(), drawBars(): read each panel's dials, call model.js, draw the two bars

layers.name: The bridge's data file
layers.what: A generated JavaScript data file, not R or Python, written by R only. The Python twin writes the same numbers as CSV under comparison/export/py/. The file holds one object, window.__BRIDGE__, with three parts. headline holds the two main estimates, the printed JR number and the two ends under (b). series holds the bridge for the explorer's one view, output (b) at each analysis's own horizon, in two ways of sizing the steps (shapley, sequential). Each is a list of 12 bars: the BSZ end, the 10 steps and the JR end. sliders holds what model.js needs to estimate any mix of dials: the two input vectors, the number of steps, the horizon settings, the inputs each dial moves with its two printed values, and the minor inputs. The explorer reads headline and sliders. Output (a) and the common horizons stay in the exports and the report.

inputs_from.what: the text of comparison-data.js, written as raw UTF-8 bytes

layers.name: Writing the pages and the data file
layers.what: build_series() turns the exported tables into the bars of every view, in display order. The BSZ end comes first (the 'bsz' bar, ends$bsz_model). Then come the steps, dropping any that is zero both ways. The JR end comes last (the 'nber' bar, ends$rauh_own). The common function returns both ends exactly, so no bar closes a model difference. render_site() fills the two pages' tokens, including the two main estimates: hl_bsz is ends$bsz_model on (b), and hl_rjkdc is the JR contract's npv_mc_nber_mean, read from endpoints.csv. It then serializes the headline, series$own$b and the sliders to JSON. write_site() writes index.html, the explorer and the data file.

layers.name: The bridge's ends and steps
layers.what: build_all() estimates everything the pages show. It loops over the horizon settings: each analysis's own horizon, then a common 5, 10, 20, 30 or 50 years or a perpetuity. With a common horizon the horizon step is not a player. In each setting it estimates score_common() at the all-BSZ inputs (v_sup, the BSZ end) and at the all-JR inputs (v_rauh). It also computes the authors' own Monte Carlo mean at the JR horizon (own_n, from rauh_nber_expectation()). For outputs (a) and (b) it then runs the two decompositions of layer 5 and stores every coalition's value (the switchboard). Each ends row records bsz_model, rauh_model, rauh_own and rauh_residual = rauh_own - rauh_model. The residual is zero by construction, because the script's own ceiling is an input; it is kept so the identity is tested.
layers.inputs: bi: the two input vectors; nber_args: the JR Monte Carlo bounds (wt_min 0, wt_max, f, C and r ranges)

inputs_from.what: the Shapley and one-order step values for each output and setting
score_common() at the two input vectors (v_sup, v_rauh) and rauh_nber_expectation() (own_n)
bi: sup and rauh, the two input vectors

layers.other_inputs: the horizon settings HORIZONS = 5, 10, 20, 30, 50 years and a perpetuity
layers.outputs: ends, own horizon, output (b): bsz_model 106.796, rauh_model -38.980, rauh_own -38.980, rauh_residual 0.000; gap = 106.796 - (-38.980) = 145.776; the 10 Shapley steps sum to -145.776
layers.method_ref: This OPA's reconciliation (PLAN.md, the common output and decision 9; DISPUTES.md for each input). Checks: test-shapley.R that the Shapley and the one-order steps sum to rauh_model - bsz_model in every setting and output; test-endpoints.R that rauh_model equals rauh_own and pins each end against the printed number; test-site.R that the steps on (b) add up to the gap between the two ends.

  so <- k$bsz$outputs; oo <- k$rjkdc$outputs; d <- k$docs
  oi <- k$rjkdc$inputs
  ggss_printed <- pick(so, "ggss_headline", "printed_value")
  bsz_row1 <- pick(so, "tab5_row1_wealth_tax_revenue")
  # The JR analysis's own Monte Carlo (NPV_dist_v8.R), as the authors ship it.
  nber_args <- list(wt_min = 0, wt_max = pick(oi, "nber_ceiling_hardcoded"),
                    f_min = pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_min"), f_max = pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_max"),
                    c_min = pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_min"), c_max = pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_max"),
                    r_min = pick(oi, "rauh_mc_r_min"), r_max = pick(oi, "rauh_mc_r_max"))
  nber_own <- function(H) do.call(rauh_nber_expectation, c(nber_args, list(H = H)))

  steps <- bridge_steps(); ids <- steps$step_id
  settings <- c("own", paste0("common_", ifelse(is.infinite(HORIZONS), "Inf", HORIZONS)))
  bridge <- list(); ends <- list(); board <- list()
  for (st in settings) {
    s2 <- sup; r2 <- rauh
    players <- ids
    if (st != "own") {
      H <- as.numeric(sub("common_", "", st))
      s2$H <- H; r2$H <- H
      players <- setdiff(ids, "horizon")

    Hr <- r2$H

layers.name: Splitting the gap into steps
layers.what: There are 10 steps. Each switches one disputed input from the BSZ value to the JR value of its September 2026 version. The share-lost step switches two together: the leavers' ratio kappa and the flat share f0. Because inputs interact, a step's size depends on when it is switched. shapley_bridge() averages each switch over every order, exactly. It estimates the model at all 2^10 = 1,024 subsets of switched inputs (coalition_values()) and weights each difference by how many orders produce it. sequential_bridge() switches them in one order, Hoopes's (sequential_order()). Both sets of steps add up to the model gap between the two input vectors. That gap is the whole gap between the two ends, since the model returns both ends exactly.
layers.inputs: sup, rauh (the two input vectors) and the list of steps

inputs_from.what: score_common(): output (b) or (a) at any mix of the two input vectors
sup and rauh, the two input vectors

layers.other_inputs: step_inputs (which arguments each step switches) and sequential_order()
layers.outputs: output (b), own horizon: 10 Shapley steps summing to -145.776 = -(145.776); the largest are litigation_survival -44.810, horizon -33.513, income_loss_share -31.333; the positive ones are avoidance +10.146
layers.method_ref: Shapley value, the standard average-over-orders decomposition. test-shapley.R checks the sum in every setting and compares with a brute-force average over orders.

layers.name: The estimating function and the JR end
layers.what: score_common() is the one function that estimates both analyses. R0 = tau x base x (1 - real-estate share) is the revenue with no behaviour. S = 1 - d_conf is the share of the base still taxed after the confirmed departures. The wealth tax is WT = R0 x (1 - alpha) x S x q, where alpha is the avoidance allowance and q the chance the Act survives litigation. The share of income tax lost is f = alpha m + (1 - alpha m)(kappa d_conf + f0): the BSZ movers' share, then the leavers' own tax on the departed base (kappa) and a flat share (f0). Output (b) is WT + X - PV, with X the extra income tax from asset sales and PV = f x C x the expected annuity. At the all-BSZ inputs S = 1 and q = 1, so WT = 0.05 x 2,307 x 0.9 = 103.815, BSZ Table 5 row 1. Output (b) adds X = 3.682 and subtracts PV = 0.701, five years of lost income tax, giving 106.796, the BSZ end. At the all-JR inputs R0 = 100.906 and S = 0.7135, so R0 x S = 72, the authors' ceiling. Then WT = 0.5 x 72 = 36, f = f0 = 0.45 and C = 4.55, so (b) = 36 - 0.45 x 4.55 x 36.620 = -38.980, the JR end. rauh_nber_expectation() (model.R lines 208-212, bridge.py lines 210-213) computes the same mean straight from the Monte Carlo's ranges: the revenue uniform on [0, 72], the share lost on [0.3, 0.6], the income tax C on [3.3, 5.8] and r on [1.5%, 4.5%], all independent. This is the last layer that computes.
layers.inputs: x: one input vector (sup at the BSZ end, rauh at the JR end); for rauh_nber_expectation(), the Monte Carlo bounds

inputs_from.what: sup: tau 0.05, W_core 2157, W_noncit 150, re 0, d_conf 0, alpha 0.1, q 1, kappa 0.334, f0 0, ...; rauh: W_core 2027.4, d_conf 0.286, q 0.5, f0 0.45, C 4.55, ...

layers.other_inputs: the Monte Carlo bounds wt_min = 0 (a literal in build.R), wt_max = 72 (contract row nber_ceiling_hardcoded), and the f, C and r ranges (contract rows nber_mc_f_*, rauh_mc_c_*, rauh_mc_r_*)
layers.method_ref: BSZ PDF p.24 (90% x 5% x $2,307B) and Table 5 row 1, p.39; Jaros and Rauh NBER c15504, the Monte Carlo in the authors' public repository (NPV_dist_v8.R). test-endpoints.R checks both ends against the printed numbers (the JR one within Monte Carlo error of the printed -38.9) and that the common function at the all-JR inputs returns the authors' expectation exactly.

r.snippet:
score_common <- function(x) {
  R0  <- x$tau * (x$W_core + x$W_noncit) * (1 - x$re)
  S   <- 1 - x$d_conf
  WT  <- R0 * (1 - x$alpha) * S * x$q
  X   <- WT * x$s * x$g * x$t_cg
  f   <- x$alpha * x$m + (1 - x$alpha * x$m) * (x$kappa * x$d_conf + x$f0)
  A   <- expected_annuity(x$H, x$r_min, x$r_max)
  PV  <- f * x$C * A
  c(a = WT, b = WT + X - PV, R0 = R0, S = S, X = X, f = f, annual_loss = f * x$C,
    annuity = A, PV = PV)
}

layers.name: The two input vectors
layers.what: bridge_inputs() builds the two settings of every disputed input. Each value is read from a contract row or a transcribed document input. The two share tau, m, g, t_cg and the discount-rate range. The BSZ base is the contract's 2,307, split into 150 of non-US-citizen residents and 2,157 of the rest. The BSZ analysis takes no departures (d_conf 0), no litigation discount (q 1), the 10% avoidance allowance and a 5 years horizon. The JR values are those of its September 2026 version. The base is the 2025 Forbes list's 1,894.8 grown 7% to 2,027.4. The real-estate share is what the person-level file nets out (0.0046). d_conf = 1 - 72 / 100.906 = 0.286 brings the revenue down to the script's ceiling after seven departures. q is 0.5, f0 and C are the midpoints of the Monte Carlo's ranges (0.45 and 4.55) and the horizon is a perpetuity.
layers.inputs: k: the two contracts and the document inputs

inputs_from.what: k$bsz, k$rjkdc (inputs and outputs tables) and k$docs, looked up row by row with pick()

layers.outputs: sup: W_core 2157, W_noncit 150, re 0, d_conf 0, alpha 0.1, q 1, kappa 0.334, f0 0, C 3.061, H 5, s 0.333; rauh: W_core 2027.4, W_noncit 0, re 0.0046, d_conf 0.286, alpha 0, q 0.5, kappa 0, f0 0.45, C 4.55, H inf, s 0

bridge_inputs <- function(k) {
  si <- k$bsz$inputs; so <- k$bsz$outputs
  oi <- k$rjkdc$inputs;   oo <- k$rjkdc$outputs
  d  <- k$docs
  W0      <- pick(si, "baseline_net_worth")
  noncit  <- pick(d, "ggss_noncitizen_wealth")
  C_sup   <- pick(si, "ca_inctax_billionaires")
  kappa_s <- (pick(si, "leavers_annual_inctax") / pick(si, "leavers_wealth")) / (C_sup / W0)
  tau     <- pick(oi, "tax_rate")
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(tau, pick(si, "tax_rate"))))
  base_r  <- pick(oi, "baseline_net_worth") * (1 + pick(oi, "nber_growth_rate"))   # 2,027.4 at 31 Dec 2026
  R0_r    <- pick(oo, "nber_domestic_grown")           # 100.906, 5% of the grown base net of real estate
  ceiling <- pick(oi, "nber_ceiling_hardcoded")        # 72, after the seven confirmed departures
  shared <- list(tau = tau, m = pick(si, "mobility_share"), g = pick(si, "gains_share"),
                 t_cg = pick(si, "ca_cg_rate"),
                 r_min = pick(oi, "rauh_mc_r_min"), r_max = pick(oi, "rauh_mc_r_max"))
  sup <- c(shared, list(
    W_noncit = noncit, W_core = W0 - noncit, re = 0, d_conf = 0,
    alpha = pick(si, "avoidance_rate"), q = 1,
    kappa = kappa_s, f0 = 0, C = C_sup, H = pick(d, "bsz_loss_horizon"),
    s = pick(si, "sell_share")))
  rauh <- c(shared, list(
    W_noncit = 0, W_core = base_r, re = 1 - R0_r / (tau * base_r),
    d_conf = 1 - ceiling / R0_r, alpha = 0, q = pick(oi, "q_litigation_survival"),
    kappa = 0, f0 = (pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_min") + pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_max")) / 2,
    C = (pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_min") + pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_max")) / 2,
    H = pick(d, "rauh_loss_horizon"), s = 0))
  list(sup = sup, rauh = rauh)
}

def bridge_inputs(k):
    si, so = k["bsz"]["inputs"], k["bsz"]["outputs"]
    oi, oo = k["rjkdc"]["inputs"], k["rjkdc"]["outputs"]
    d = k["docs"]
    W0 = pick(si, "baseline_net_worth")
    noncit = pick(d, "ggss_noncitizen_wealth")
    C_sup = pick(si, "ca_inctax_billionaires")
    kappa_s = (pick(si, "leavers_annual_inctax") / pick(si, "leavers_wealth")) / (C_sup / W0)
    tau = pick(oi, "tax_rate")
    assert abs(tau - pick(si, "tax_rate")) < 1e-12
    base_r = pick(oi, "baseline_net_worth") * (1 + pick(oi, "nber_growth_rate"))
    R0_r = pick(oo, "nber_domestic_grown")
    ceiling = pick(oi, "nber_ceiling_hardcoded")
    shared = {"tau": tau, "m": pick(si, "mobility_share"), "g": pick(si, "gains_share"),
              "t_cg": pick(si, "ca_cg_rate"),
              "r_min": pick(oi, "rauh_mc_r_min"), "r_max": pick(oi, "rauh_mc_r_max")}
    sup = dict(shared, W_noncit=noncit, W_core=W0 - noncit, re=0.0, d_conf=0.0,
               alpha=pick(si, "avoidance_rate"), q=1.0,
               kappa=kappa_s, f0=0.0, C=C_sup,
               H=pick(d, "bsz_loss_horizon"), s=pick(si, "sell_share"))
    rauh = dict(shared, W_noncit=0.0, W_core=base_r, re=1 - R0_r / (tau * base_r),
                d_conf=1 - ceiling / R0_r, alpha=0.0, q=pick(oi, "q_litigation_survival"),
                kappa=0.0, f0=(pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_min") + pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_max")) / 2,
                C=(pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_min") + pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_max")) / 2,
                H=pick(d, "rauh_loss_horizon"), s=0.0)
    return sup, rauh

layers.name: The raw source: the two export contracts
layers.what: The comparison reads exactly three kinds of file. The first is each analysis's export contract (export/r/inputs.csv and outputs.csv, written by that analysis's own pipeline for others to read). The second is the values transcribed from the PDFs with their page (comparison/data/document-inputs.csv). The third is Hoopes's digitized figure. pick() looks up one row and fails loudly if it is missing or duplicated. The chain stops here: what is behind each contract row is each analysis's own chain.

read_contracts <- function(root = comparison_root()) {
  side <- function(s) list(
    inputs  = read_csv_plain(file.path(root, s, "export", "r", "inputs.csv")),
    outputs = read_csv_plain(file.path(root, s, "export", "r", "outputs.csv")))
  docs <- read_csv_plain(file.path(root, "comparison", "data", "document-inputs.csv"))
  docs$value <- as.numeric(docs$value)          # "Inf" parses to Inf
  list(bsz = side("bsz-analysis"),
       rjkdc = side("rjkdc-analysis"),
       docs       = docs,
       hoopes     = read_csv_plain(file.path(root, "comparison", "data", "hoopes-fig2.csv")))
}

# Look up one value, failing loudly if the contract row is missing or duplicated.
pick <- function(df, id, col = "value", key = NULL) {
  key <- key %||% names(df)[1]
  hit <- df[df[[key]] == id, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(hit) != 1) stop(sprintf("expected exactly one row '%s', found %d", id, nrow(hit)))
  hit[[col]]
}
